summary: Defines URI fragment identifiers for text/csv, to refer to rows, columns or cells, singly or in ranges. This makes it possible to link directly to part of a CSV file.

eli5.summary: Addresses for spreadsheet pieces, such as row three.

questions: refer to a cell in csv
how to link to a row in a csv file
what is a uri fragment identifier
subtitle: How to link straight to a row, column or cell of a CSV file using a URI fragment.

tldr.problem: A URI can point to a whole CSV file, but not to a particular row, column or cell inside it.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines fragment identifiers for text/csv: row=, col= and cell= selections, with single positions, ranges, the * symbol for the last item, and semicolon-separated multiple selections.
tldr.outcome: Clients that do not understand the fragment simply treat the URI as pointing to the whole file, so it can be adopted gradually. The RFC updates the text/csv registration from RFC 4180.

today: RFC 7111 is an Informational Independent Submission that updates RFC 4180, the text/csv registration. It has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC.

sections.title: Why CSV Needs Fragment Identifiers
sections.content:
A URI may end in a fragment identifier after a number sign. It is interpreted by the client after the resource is retrieved, and its meaning depends on the media type of what came back. Many media types have no fragment method, so this memo defines one for text/csv, in the same spirit as the text/plain fragments in RFC 5147.

Use cases include selecting a part for visual rendering, stream processing, making assertions about a value (provenance, confidence, comments) and data integration.

Deployment is gentle. A client that does not support the fragment still retrieves the whole file, which is a reasonable fallback. Because the fragment is evaluated only in the client, a server cannot tell whether a requester used one.
sections.eli5: A normal link points to the whole spreadsheet. This adds a way to point at one row, column or box in it.

sections.title: Row, Column and Cell Selections
sections.content:
Three methods exist: row, col and cell. Positions count from 1, and an asterisk as in row=5-* means the last row or column. The RFC's example table has seven rows including a header, and three columns (date, temperature, place).

  • #row=4 selects the fourth row; #row=5-7 or #row=5-* selects a range.
  • #col=2 selects the second column; #col=1-2 the first two.
  • #cell=4,1 selects the cell in row 4, column 1; #cell=4,1-6,2 selects the region from the upper left cell to the lower right cell.

Several selections of one kind can be joined with semicolons, for example #row=3;6, which may produce a disjoint fragment. User agents decide how to handle disjoint fragments.
sections.eli5: Row three, column two, or a rectangle from here to there. Write the numbers after the hash sign.

sections.title: Processing Rules for Clients
sections.content:
A fragment with a syntax error MUST be ignored. Clients MUST NOT try to correct or guess, and MAY report the error.

  • A single selection pointing to a non-existing row or column MUST be ignored.
  • A range extending past the end of the CSV MUST be treated as ending at the actual size.
  • An inverse range such as #row=10-5 MUST be ignored.

Each specification is processed independently, so one ignored part does not break the others. For the example file, #row=1-2;5-4;13-16 identifies just the first two rows. Overlapping parts, such as #row=3-6;4-5, may be kept as two parts or merged, at the user agent's choice.
sections.eli5: If the directions make no sense, the client skips them. If they point past the end, it stops at the last row.

sections.title: IANA and Security Considerations
sections.content:
IANA added a reference to this specification in the text/csv media type registration. The registration was copied from RFC 4180 with added fragment identifier and security text. The change needed IESG approval, because the IESG is the change controller of the registration.

Security-wise, text/csv is passive text, though malicious data could exploit bugs such as buffer overruns, and the format gives no confidentiality or integrity protection. Software that supports fragments behaves differently from software that does not, and different software may display fragments differently. Such misunderstandings could be exploited in ways similar to spoofing or phishing. Implementers should also read the security considerations of RFC 3986 and RFC 3987.
sections.eli5: The official list of file types now mentions the new bookmarks. Because programs may show the same bookmark differently, people could be confused or tricked.

data.title: csv-fragment syntax
data.code:
csv-fragment =  rowsel / colsel / cellsel
rowsel       =  "row=" singlespec 0*( ";" singlespec)
colsel       =  "col=" singlespec 0*( ";" singlespec)
cellsel      =  "cell=" cellspec 0*( ";" cellspec)
singlespec   =  position [ "-" position ]
cellspec     =  cellrow "," cellcol [ "-" cellrow "," cellcol ]
cellrow      =  position
cellcol      =  position
position     =  number / "*"
number       =  1*( DIGIT )
